unit.title: This season, live
unit.summary: Weekly templates driven by live data: previews, recaps, title picture, driver and team form.

lessons.title: This weekend: what to watch
lessons.objective: Read a race preview: circuit type, tyre picks and what matters most.

payload.prompt: A preview says: walls close, little run-off, pole matters. What kind of circuit?

options.text: A street circuit
options.explanation: Right. Tight, bumpy, walled tracks make passing hard, so qualifying and track position matter most.

options.text: A high-speed, flat-out circuit
options.explanation: High-speed tracks have long straights and fast corners, and run-off is usually generous.

options.text: A balanced circuit with no particular trait
options.explanation: Balanced tracks do not have this walls-and-pole character.

explanation.correct: Close walls, little run-off and a premium on pole are classic street-circuit signs, like Monaco or Singapore.
explanation.incorrect: Close walls and little room to pass point to a street circuit, where track position is gold.
explanation.sayThisLine: It is a street circuit, so qualifying matters.

payload.prompt: A preview warns of a very hot race. Which compound helps with tyre wear?

options.text: The hard (white), which lasts longest in the heat.
options.explanation: Right. Hard tyres are slower per lap but wear less, which is useful when heat is hurting the tyres.

options.text: The soft (red), because it is always the best.
options.explanation: Softs give the most grip but wear fastest, and heat makes that worse.

options.text: The intermediate (green), because it is cooler.
options.explanation: Intermediates are for damp tracks, and they would be destroyed on a hot dry one.

explanation.correct: Heat raises tyre wear, so harder compounds that last longer become more attractive. Teams weigh that against the pace they lose.
explanation.incorrect: Hot tracks punish soft tyres. The harder compounds are slower per lap but survive longer.
explanation.sayThisLine: It is hot, so the hards might last longest.

payload.prompt: On a sprint weekend, how much practice do teams get?

scene.alt: Text only: a sprint weekend has sprint qualifying, a sprint race, then qualifying and the Grand Prix.

explanation.correct: A sprint weekend has just one practice session, because the sprint qualifying and sprint race fill the rest of the schedule. Teams have to get the car right quickly.
explanation.incorrect: A normal weekend has three practice sessions. On a sprint weekend there is only one, so set-up choices are made with very little data.
explanation.sayThisLine: Only one practice on a sprint weekend, so no room for mistakes.

payload.prompt: Friday is cool but Sunday will be hot. How do you set up?

situation.narrative: Friday practice is on a cool, low-grip track. The forecast says Sunday's race will be much hotter.

options.label: Aim for Sunday's conditions and use Friday to learn the car.
options.consequence: Friday times look slower, but the set-up will be closer to what the car needs in the race, and the team learns how it reacts to change.
considerations: The race is where the big points are.
Heat changes tyre wear and balance, so conditions matter.

options.label: Tune for Friday and fix it later.
options.consequence: Friday looks good, but the car may be wrong when it gets hot, with little time to adjust.
considerations: Friday is a guide, not the target.
There is limited time before the set-up locks.

options.label: Split the difference and aim at Saturday qualifying.
options.consequence: Qualifying is sorted, but Sunday's heat may still catch the team out.
considerations: The race still needs its own plan.

payload.expertNote: Teams use Friday to understand the car's sensitivity and plan for the conditions they expect on race day.
payload.sayThisLine: Friday is a guide. Sunday is the test.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Tyre deg is going to be the story this weekend.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: The tyres will wear quickly, so stops and stint lengths will decide the race.
options.explanation: Right. Deg means degradation: how fast the tyres lose grip.

options.text: The tyres will be very hard to get hold of.
options.explanation: Deg is about wear, not supply.

options.text: The track surface is about to be replaced.
options.explanation: Deg refers to tyre degradation, not the track itself.

payload.translation: Deg is short for degradation. If it is high, tyres fade fast, so strategy becomes the story.

followUps.line: Which tyre does she think wears worst?
followUps.why: A good follow-up that keeps the conversation going.
High degradation often means more stops, but not always.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you are not sure, ask which tyre she expects to struggle.

lessons.title: Last race in plain English
lessons.objective: Decode last race's result, strategy calls and controversies.

payload.prompt: A chaser pits a lap before the leader. When does the undercut work?

options.text: When fresh tyres make the chaser quick enough to come out ahead after the leader stops.
options.explanation: Right. The gain comes from pace on new tyres before the leader pits.

options.text: When the pit stop takes under two seconds.
options.explanation: A quick stop helps, but the undercut depends on the pace on new tyres.

options.text: When both cars pit on the same lap.
options.explanation: If they pit together, there is no undercut.

explanation.correct: The chaser pits first, gains time on fresh tyres while the leader is on old ones, then comes out ahead once the leader stops.
explanation.incorrect: An undercut needs the chaser to be noticeably quicker on fresh tyres than the leader on old ones.
explanation.sayThisLine: The undercut worked because the new tyres were quick.

payload.prompt: A car pits just as the safety car comes out. Good luck or bad luck?

scene.alt: Text only: a car makes a pit stop while the field is slow behind the safety car.

explanation.correct: Under a safety car the field is slow, so a stop costs roughly half as much time as normal. Pitting just as it comes out is a big win.
explanation.incorrect: Safety cars slow everyone, so a pit stop costs much less. That is why pitting at the right moment is such a gift.
explanation.sayThisLine: He got a cheap stop under the safety car.

payload.prompt: A driver finishes second and gets a five-second time penalty. What happens to their result?

options.text: They stay second; penalty points are added to their licence.
options.explanation: Penalty points and time penalties are separate things.

options.text: Five seconds are added to their race time, potentially dropping their place.
options.explanation: Right; a five-second penalty can change the final order.

options.text: They are disqualified from this race.
options.explanation: That would be a harsher penalty like a black flag.

explanation.correct: Right. A time penalty is added to the race time; it can swing the finishing order if the margin is tight.
explanation.incorrect: A time penalty adds seconds to the final race time, not licence points. Five seconds can drop a driver from second to fourth if others are close.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: He was leading by ten seconds and then a DNF. That car was the fastest out there.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: He retired from the lead, so the pace earned him nothing.
options.explanation: DNF means did not finish. A retirement scores zero, however fast the car was.

options.text: He finished first but lost the title.
options.explanation: DNF means he did not finish, so there was no win.

options.text: He was given a penalty but kept racing.
options.explanation: A penalty is different. DNF means he stopped racing.

payload.translation: He had to retire from a commanding lead. Points only come from finishing, so a fast car scores nothing if it stops.

followUps.line: Was it a mechanical failure or a crash?
followUps.why: The cause tells you whether it was bad luck, a mistake or a reliability issue.

followUps.line: How many points did that cost him?
followUps.why: A win is worth 25, so the gap can grow quickly.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Do not guess the cause. Asking what went wrong is a real-fan question.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: The pit wall gambled on the undercut and it paid off this time.

payload.question: What did the strategist do?

options.text: Pitted earlier than the rival to jump ahead on fresh tyres.
options.explanation: That is an undercut, and she says it worked.

options.text: Stayed out longer than the rival to gain clear air.
options.explanation: That is an overcut, the opposite idea.

options.text: Tried it and it failed.
options.explanation: She said it paid off, so it worked.

payload.translation: The team stopped first, hoping fresh tyres would let the driver lap faster than the rival and come out ahead.

followUps.line: Did the other team see it coming?
followUps.why: A good question about whether the rival could have covered the stop.

followUps.line: How many seconds did it gain?
followUps.why: The gain on fresh tyres shows whether it was a clear success.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you are unsure who did what, ask which driver pitted first.

lessons.title: The championship picture
lessons.objective: Read standings and work out who can still win and what they need.

payload.prompt: The leader is 60 points clear with two normal races left. Is it over?

options.text: Yes. Two wins are worth 50, so the chaser cannot catch up.
options.explanation: Right. Two Grand Prix wins give 50 points, which is fewer than the 60-point gap.

options.text: No. The chaser can win both and catch up.
options.explanation: Winning both gains 50 points on a rival who scores nothing, so 60 is out of reach.

options.text: Not yet, because fastest lap gives extra points.
options.explanation: There is no fastest-lap point since 2025.

explanation.correct: The most a driver can gain on another in a normal race is 25, if he wins and the rival scores nothing. Over two races that is 50, less than the 60-point gap.
explanation.incorrect: Each normal race can swing at most 25 points. Two races is 50, so a 60-point gap cannot be closed.
explanation.sayThisLine: He needs fifty and there is only fifty on offer, so it is over.

payload.prompt: Most points a chaser can gain on a rival in one normal Grand Prix?

explanation.correct: 25 points: a win scores 25, and if the rival scores nothing the chaser gains the full amount. That is the number title-maths starts from.
explanation.incorrect: The best case is a win for 25 points against a rival who scores zero, which is a 25-point swing. Sprints add a bit more.
explanation.sayThisLine: A win against a retirement is a twenty-five point swing.

payload.prompt: In the constructors' title, whose points count?

scene.alt: Text only: a team has two drivers who both score points in a race.

explanation.correct: Both drivers' points are added together for the team. That is why having two strong drivers, and reliable cars, matters.
explanation.incorrect: The constructors' title adds the points of both drivers, not just the better one.
explanation.sayThisLine: Both cars have to score for the team title.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: If he wins the next three and the leader finishes fifth, it is suddenly a fight.

payload.question: What is she working out?

options.text: Wins plus a bad run for the leader can close a gap fast.
options.explanation: Right. A win is 25 and fifth is 10, so each such race swings 15 points.

options.text: Points are awarded only for wins.
options.explanation: Points go down to tenth place.

options.text: The leader will lose the title for certain.
options.explanation: It only narrows the gap. Nothing is certain.

payload.translation: One driver winning and the other scoring less can shrink a gap quickly. Three such races would be a 45-point swing.

followUps.why: A good prompt to do the sum: 25 minus 10, three times, is 45.
The number of races left decides whether it is possible.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need the exact standings. Asking how far behind he is works.

lessons.title: {{driver}} this season
lessons.objective: Explain how {{driver}} is performing this season and why.

payload.prompt: A driver qualifies behind his teammate but beats him on Sunday. What might explain it?

options.text: Better race pace or tyre care, or strategy that worked out.
options.explanation: Right. One lap and a race are different tests, and strategy can change the result.

options.text: The teammate has a slower car.
options.explanation: Teammates share a car, so that is not the explanation.

options.text: Qualifying does not count for anything.
options.explanation: Qualifying decides the grid, which matters. It just is not the whole story.

explanation.correct: Race pace, tyre management and strategy can all beat a better grid slot. That is why fans look at Saturday and Sunday separately.
explanation.incorrect: A driver can be slower over one lap but stronger over a race. Strategy and luck also play a part.
explanation.sayThisLine: He was slower in qualifying but better on Sunday.

payload.prompt: Teammates are a consistent six tenths apart in qualifying. Big gap or small?

scene.alt: Text only: a qualifying gap between two teammates in the same car.

explanation.correct: Six tenths in the same car is large. Qualifying gaps between teammates are often a few hundredths to a few tenths, so this is a real pace difference.
explanation.incorrect: In the same car, six tenths every weekend is a large and consistent gap, not noise.
explanation.sayThisLine: Six tenths in the same car is a serious gap.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: On Sundays {{driver}} is usually quicker than on Saturdays.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: {{driver}} looks stronger over a race than over one lap.
options.explanation: Right. She is separating race pace from one-lap pace.

options.text: {{driver}} only scores points on race day.
options.explanation: Points are scored only in races, but that is not her point.

options.text: {{driver}} never qualifies well.
options.explanation: She says usually quicker on Sunday, not that qualifying is bad.

payload.translation: She is saying {{driver}} tends to do better in the race than in qualifying.

followUps.line: Is that tyre care or just patience?
followUps.why: Race pace usually comes from looking after the tyres and reading the race.

followUps.line: Does a better grid slot fix it?
followUps.why: A better start position usually helps a driver who is strong in races.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can respond without opinions on the driver. Ask what she has noticed.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: {{driver}} has had the pace, but a couple of DNFs have cost a lot of points.

payload.question: What is her point?

options.text: Speed is there, but retirements score zero and hurt the points total.
options.explanation: Right. A DNF costs the whole race, however fast the car was.

options.text: {{driver}} is not good at overtaking.
options.explanation: Her point is about retirements, not overtaking.

options.text: {{driver}}'s teammate is faster.
options.explanation: She did not mention the teammate.

payload.translation: She means {{driver}} is quick but losing points because of retirements.

followUps.line: Was it the car or an accident?
followUps.why: The cause decides whether it is bad luck, a mistake or reliability.
It turns the complaint into a number you can compare.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not have to know the story. Asking what happened is a great start.

lessons.title: {{team}} this season
lessons.objective: Explain {{team}}'s form and what to watch in their race.

payload.prompt: Suppose a team is third, 30 points behind second, with eight races left. Still in it?

options.text: Yes. Eight races offer many points, so 30 is within reach.
options.explanation: Right. A race can swing more than 25 points, so the gap can close.

options.text: No. Thirty points is too many to ever catch.
options.explanation: Eight races gives a lot of scope. It is a gap, not a wall.

options.text: Only if the top two drivers retire.
options.explanation: It helps, but it is not required.

explanation.correct: A team can gain plenty on a rival over eight races through better pace, reliability and both cars scoring. Thirty points is small in that context.
explanation.incorrect: With eight races left, 30 points is not decisive. Both cars scoring consistently can close it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Thirty points with eight races to go is alive.

payload.prompt: In a new rules era, does last year's form guarantee this year's pace?

scene.alt: Text only: new rules mean new cars.

explanation.correct: New rules mean new cars, so the pecking order can change a lot. That is why form from the last era says less about {{team}} and everyone else.
explanation.incorrect: When the rules change, teams start with new designs. Past success is no guarantee.
explanation.sayThisLine: New rules can shuffle the order.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: {{team}} brought a big upgrade and the pace jumped two tenths.

payload.question: What probably helped?

options.text: A new aero part, like a wing or a floor, that improved performance.
options.explanation: Right. Mid-season upgrades are most often aerodynamic.

options.text: A new driver joined the team.
options.explanation: An upgrade is a car part, not a driver.

options.text: The rules changed in their favour.
options.explanation: Rule changes apply to every team.

payload.translation: She says {{team}} brought new parts that made the car about two tenths quicker.

followUps.line: Is it an aero or a power unit update?
followUps.why: Different updates matter for different reasons, and it shows you are paying attention.
Teams bring upgrades all the time, so the gain can shrink.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can ask what the upgrade actually was. Most fans like explaining it.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: We are fast enough, but we keep losing cars to failures. If we finish every race, we are a lot higher.

payload.question: What is she telling you?

options.text: {{team}} has pace, but reliability is costing points.
options.explanation: Right. Pace and finishing are both needed.

options.text: {{team}} is guaranteed to win if they finish.
options.explanation: She is saying it would help, not that it is guaranteed.

options.text: {{team}} should stop racing.
options.explanation: She is frustrated, not giving up.

payload.translation: She means the car is quick but too many retirements are costing {{team}} points.

followUps.why: The cause tells you whether it is the car, the power unit or something else.
It shows you care about how they solve the problem.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need the technical detail. Ask what keeps breaking.

lessons.title: The 2026 rules, still in motion
lessons.objective: Follow mid-season tweaks to the regulations and why teams argue about them.

payload.prompt: The FIA issues a technical directive mid-season. Is that unusual?

options.text: No. Directives often close loopholes that teams find once the cars are racing.
options.explanation: Right. Teams push the edges of the rulebook, and the FIA clarifies how rules will be policed.

options.text: Yes. The rules are locked all season.
options.explanation: The regulations are fixed, but the FIA can clarify how they are applied.

options.text: Yes. It only happens when someone is disqualified.
options.explanation: Directives come from rule questions, not from disqualifications.

explanation.correct: A technical directive is an FIA note on how a rule will be policed. It is common for loopholes such as bending wings.
explanation.incorrect: Directives are a normal tool, used mid-season to clarify or close loopholes.
explanation.sayThisLine: They closed a loophole with a directive.

payload.prompt: When is ADUO assessed?

scene.alt: Text only: ADUO is the engine makers' catch-up mechanism.

explanation.correct: ADUO is reviewed at three checkpoints, after rounds 6, 12 and 18. Engine makers who are far enough behind can get extra upgrade chances.
explanation.incorrect: ADUO is checked during the season, at three points, not just once at the start.
explanation.sayThisLine: ADUO gets checked after rounds six, twelve and eighteen.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Some engine makers are arguing about the compression ratio again.

payload.question: What is the dispute about?

options.text: How tightly the engine squeezes its air-fuel mix, and how the limit is measured.
options.explanation: Right. Compression ratio is a limit, and the row is about checking it cold or hot.

options.text: How much fuel a car can carry.
options.explanation: Fuel is covered by a separate rule, not this one.

options.text: Which team gets extra tyres.
options.explanation: Tyres have nothing to do with it.

payload.translation: Engine makers are arguing about how the compression ratio limit is checked, since the ratio can change once an engine is hot.

followUps.why: The FIA moved to control the ratio hot as well as cold from 1 June 2026.
It affects how much power an engine can make, which affects the pecking order.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: It is a technical row. Asking who is upset and why is enough.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: The FIA keeps tweaking the 2026 rules mid-season. Why can't they just leave them?

payload.question: What is the fair answer?

options.text: New rules throw up surprises once teams race them, so the FIA adjusts for safety or racing quality.
options.explanation: Right. The real cars show problems the paperwork did not.

options.text: They change them at random to annoy teams.
options.explanation: Changes are made through discussion and votes, not at random.

options.text: They change them so one team always wins.
options.explanation: That would be unfair, and teams would object.

payload.translation: When rules are new, they are tested in real racing. If problems appear, the FIA and teams adjust them.

followUps.why: A good question that keeps you following the story.
Rule changes can help some teams more than others, which is why teams argue.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can say you do not know the latest tweak. Asking about it is fine.

lessons.title: Silly season: who is moving
lessons.objective: Follow driver-market stories and upcoming seat changes.

payload.prompt: Silly season peaks in which part of the season?

options.text: Early season, before the title is decided
options.explanation: Early news does happen, but it is quieter.

options.text: Mid-season, when the title picture clarifies
options.explanation: Right. Teams know who is quick and who is free to move.

options.text: After the season ends
options.explanation: Announcements come, but the buzz is mid-season.

explanation.correct: Right. Once teams know their competitive position, they plan for next year. Speculation and signings peak mid-season.
explanation.incorrect: Silly season is loudest mid-season when teams know their form and start plotting signings.

payload.prompt: When is a driver move official?

scene.alt: Text only: rumours and announcements in the driver market.

explanation.correct: Stories are often right, but a move is official when the team or driver confirms it. Until then, it is silly season talk.
explanation.incorrect: A report is not an announcement. A move is official when the team or driver confirms it.
explanation.sayThisLine: It is not official until the team says so.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: A young driver has just won F2. Is there a seat for him next year?

payload.question: What decides whether he gets an F1 drive?

options.text: The F2 title, enough super licence points, and a seat actually being free.
options.explanation: Right. Merit, licence and timing all matter.

options.text: Only the F2 title.
options.explanation: Plenty of F2 champions have had to wait for a seat.

options.text: Whether the team likes his surname.
options.explanation: Results and licence points matter more, along with backing.

payload.translation: F2 success earns super licence points, but there are only 20 or so seats, so a good junior may have to wait.

followUps.line: Which teams have a seat free?
followUps.why: It shows you are tracking where the openings are.

followUps.line: Does his junior programme have a team?
followUps.why: Academy ties often decide where a young driver lands.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: It is fine to say you do not know which seats are open. Ask.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Everyone is talking about his contract. Does he stay or chase a bigger seat?

payload.question: What is she asking about?

options.text: Whether he extends with his team or moves to a stronger one.
options.explanation: Right. It is the classic silly season choice.

options.text: Whether he can afford a new contract.
options.explanation: Teams pay drivers. Drivers do not pay for contracts.

options.text: Whether he will become a team principal.
options.explanation: That is a different future.

payload.translation: A driver on a good run is weighing loyalty to his team against a move to one with a better car.

followUps.why: Opinions are a friendly follow-up, and they keep the chat going.
It asks about rumours without stating anything as fact.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rumours are not facts. Treat them as guesses.

lessons.title: Circuit primer: {{region}} and the next race
lessons.objective: Prepare for the next race: layout, circuit personality and likely strategy.

payload.prompt: A primer says long straights and few slow corners. What does that favour?

options.text: Low-drag set-ups and strong power, with lots of slipstream battles.
options.explanation: Right. Straights reward low drag, power and the tow.

options.text: Maximum downforce with big wings.
options.explanation: Big wings create drag, which costs speed on straights.

options.text: Soft tyres only.
options.explanation: Tyre choice depends on wear, not on straights.

explanation.correct: On a track of long straights, low-drag set-ups and power matter most, and slipstreaming is a big part of passing.
explanation.incorrect: Long straights favour low drag and power. Big wings would slow the car down there.
explanation.sayThisLine: It is a low-drag track, so top speed matters.

payload.prompt: Tap where following closely is hardest because of dirty air.

diagram.alt: Stylised circuit outline with a long straight on the left ending in a tight hairpin, and a fast sweeping curve on the right.

explanation.correct: In a fast corner the car ahead's wake steals the follower's downforce when it needs grip most, so staying close is hardest there.
explanation.incorrect: Dirty air matters most in fast corners, where the follower depends on downforce. Slow hairpins and pit entry are less affected.
explanation.sayThisLine: He could not stay close in the fast corners.

payload.prompt: Tap where cars leave the track to pit.

diagram.alt: Stylised circuit outline with a long straight on the left ending in a tight hairpin, and a fast sweeping curve on the right.

explanation.correct: The pit entry is where cars peel off for a stop. Its position and the speed limit in the lane decide how much time a stop costs at each track.
explanation.incorrect: Cars leave the racing line at the pit entry, not at a corner. A long pit lane means a bigger pit loss.
explanation.sayThisLine: A long pit lane makes a stop more expensive.

payload.prompt: Tyres last long at a track with a big pit loss. One stop or two?

scene.alt: Text only: a long pit lane makes every stop expensive, and tyres wear slowly.

explanation.correct: Long-lasting tyres and an expensive pit stop both point to one stop. Fewer stops means less time lost in the pit lane.
explanation.incorrect: When tyres last and stops cost a lot, teams usually choose one stop rather than two.
explanation.sayThisLine: Big pit loss and slow wear means one stop.

payload.prompt: Practice shows slow tyre wear. One stop or two for {{region|the next race}}?

situation.narrative: Friday long runs suggest the tyres last about 40 laps. The race is 60 laps long. Friday is cooler than the forecast for Sunday.

options.label: Plan one stop, but be ready to add a second if it is hotter.
options.consequence: You save time if the tyres hold, and you have a fallback if heat wears them faster.
considerations: Sunday is hotter, so wear could be higher.
A flexible plan adapts to conditions.

options.label: Commit to one stop no matter what.
options.consequence: If the tyres wear faster in the heat, you hit the cliff and lose a lot of time.
considerations: Friday is cooler than the race.

options.label: Plan two stops to be safe.
options.consequence: Safe on tyres, but you give up about 20 seconds you may not need to lose.
considerations: You can always add a stop later.

payload.expertNote: Friday data is a guide. Teams plan a main strategy and keep a fallback ready for conditions changing on race day.
payload.sayThisLine: Friday is cooler, so keep a second stop in your back pocket.
